claims.text: Atomic-scale lattice distortion caused by a highly disordered chemical environment is the dominant mechanism governing strength and deformation or failure in multi-component concentrated alloys.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous and has a random distribution of constituent elements.
Controlled heat treatments can vary local atomic ordering without changing overall alloy composition.
Chemical disorder produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions produce spatial variations in elastic moduli.
The random arrangement of multiple principal elements creates heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Heterogeneous lattice distortions pin or impede dislocations.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy yield strength.
Heat-treatment-induced local chemical ordering reduces chemical disorder and lattice distortion.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers yield strength.
Changing local ordering and lattice distortion alters deformation and failure behavior.
Relative to a maximally disordered baseline, more locally ordered alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, more locally ordered alloys will exhibit altered deformation modes, including less abrupt failure.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when phase segregation, grain-boundary-dominated deformation, and thermal microstructural instability are absent or negligible.
Heat treatments may cause phase transformations or nanoscale segregation that confound the ordering comparison.
Identically composed alloys receiving different heat treatments provide the proposed controlled comparison.
A lack of consistent measurable changes in strength, deformation mode, or dislocation activity after modifying local ordering would falsify the hypothesis.
